title: Alien life in sulfuric acid? A surprising possible alternative to water
site_name: EarthSky | Updates on your cosmos and world
excerpt: Alien life in sulfuric acid? Recent studies show how some kinds of organic molecules and even DNA can survive in the highly corrosive acid.
content:
• Could there be alien life in sulfuric acid? Could living organisms use sulfuric acid in place of water?
  • Planetary scientist Sara Seager and her son conducted experiments to try to answer those questions.
  • Surprisingly, they found that some organic molecules could indeed survive in sulfuric acid, including forms of DNA with peptides instead of sugar molecules.

Alien life in sulfuric acid?

Life as we know it requires water. But could other fluids work as well as a foundation for life, maybe even sulfuric acid? The idea sounds far-fetched. But maybe it’s not? Could some forms of life survive or even thrive in acid?

Sulfuric acid is famously corrosive and lethal to almost all life on Earth. In pop culture, it’s a go-to plot device for villains, usually stored in a steaming, open vat conveniently placed beneath a rickety catwalk, ready to dissolve an unlucky henchman down to the bone.

So it seems surprising that, in experiments that began in the summer of 2020, prominent planetary scientist Sara Seager and her son Max Seager decided to challenge the idea of sulfuric acid as being unsurvivable for life forms. They wondered, could sulfuric acid — in some circumstances — support life?

Natalie Wolchover wrote about the intriguing implications for The New York Times on November 10, 2026.

The experiments

Seager was helping to design a new mission to Venus, which has cloud filled with droplets of sulfuric acid. She asked Max to find out how different metals and ceramic would react to sulfuric acid. But most of that information was already available online.

Max had some other ideas. First, he put an ant in the acid. It didn’t fare well as Max said:

The poor ant kind of just liquefied. That led into this bigger series of experiments.

Then he used a rhododendron leaf. But not much happened. Why? The leaf had a coating of wax that protected it.

A carbon and water bias

For many decades, scientists have thought that life must be based on carbon and water. That included well-known scientist and space advocate Carl Sagan. He wrote in his book Cosmos:

 I am, reluctantly, a self-confessed carbon chauvinist. I am also a water chauvinist.

Vikki Meadows is an astrobiologist at the University of Washington in Seattle and the NASA-funded Virtual Planetary Laboratory. She is open-minded about other fluids for life, saying:

It’s worthwhile to look at alternative solvents.

But she is focused on what can be detected now, in water:

So, I’m still Team Water for that reason.

Sulfuric acid as an elixir of life?

Max went on to study chemistry at the nearby Worcester Polytechnic Institute, and the experiments continued, although more sporadically. Using an old spectrometer, Max and Sara studied what kinds of organic molecules might be stable in sulfuric acid, if any.

In 2023, they found something interesting regarding DNA (Deoxyribonucleic acid). The molecular “letters” of DNA — adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine — are the genetic code of all living organisms on Earth. And in the experiments, they remained intact in sulfuric acid. How is that possible?

Those letters are lined up along a “backbone” of phosphate and sugar molecules. And sulfuric acid loves to “eat” — or rather destroy — sugar. But according to the experiments, if a form of DNA didn’t have sugar, it would survive in the sulfuric acid.

Later, in 2025, the researchers found that an alternative form of DNA, with peptides instead of sugars, stayed intact in the sulfuric acid. In fact, the peptides folded into the kinds of 3-dimensional shapes that other biomolecules do that are needed for biological functions.

Collaborator Janusz Petkowski at Wroclaw University of Science and Technology in Poland told The New York Times:

The stability of organic molecules in sulfuric acid is a rule, not an exception.

Implications for Venus

The results have implications not only for distant exoplanets, but also much closer to home … on Venus. Venus’ thick clouds contain droplets of sulfuric acid. (Although a study from 2025 suggested that there is less acid and more water than previously thought).

So, could microscopic life exist in those droplets? Maybe. Seagers’ findings, plus other evidence that amino acids could survive in those clouds — where it is cooler and more earthlike than the hellish surface below — make it a tantalizing possibility.

And, of course, there’s the phosphine saga. This potential biosignature first reported back in 2020, might be evidence for just such microbial life floating in Venus’ clouds. But the jury is currently still out.

And if you’re still thinking all of this is far-fetched, remember Dr. Ian Malcolm’s famous line from Jurassic Park:

Life finds a way.

Bottom line: Alien life in sulfuric acid? Recent studies show how some kinds of organic molecules and even DNA can survive in the highly corrosive acid.

Via The New York Times
